Bharat (India) is consuming differently. Everyday essentials still matter, but the choices around them are becoming more considered. Families are looking for better nutrition, trusted quality, greater convenience and products rooted in tradition, yet relevant to modern lifestyles.
Our trusted brands, wide distribution network and focus on innovation connect these strengths to everyday life. Collectively, they allow us to serve changing needs without losing sight of affordability, accessibility and well-being.

Our trusted brands, wide distribution network and focus on innovation connect these strengths to everyday life. Collectively, they allow us to serve changing needs without losing sight of affordability, accessibility and well-being.
Patanjali Foods is evolving with this shift. From a predominantly edible oil business, we have grown into an FMCG- led consumer company spanning foods, nutrition, home and personal care. Our portfolio serves mass, value and premium segments, across ages, regions and occasions, bringing together natural ingredients and contemporary formats to help more people lead healthier, more joyful lives.
Nourishing Bharat captures this larger purpose. It reflects how we are helping rewrite the consumption story, from what Bharat buys to how it is produced, delivered and experienced. A story of healthier choices, stronger livelihoods, wider opportunity and enduring value.
Yet nourishment begins long before a product reaches the shelf. Through our expanding oil palm plantations, we are strengthening domestic sourcing, supporting farmers and building a more integrated edible oil value chain. This backward integration adds resilience to our business while advancing India’s journey towards greater self-reliance.

From the Kitchen to the Wider Home

From the Kitchen to the Wider Home
The journey from the kitchen to the wider home reflects the evolution of Patanjali Foods itself: from serving important everyday needs to becoming a more complete part of everyday life.
Nourishing Bharat by bringing well-being into more of the choices households make every day.

For consumers, the impact is greater choice across nourishment, well-being and care. For Patanjali Foods, it means a deeper consumer relationship and a more resilient business, with higher-margin FMCG categories playing an increasingly important role in our earnings mix. Supported by established brands, an extensive distribution ecosystem and our proprietary network of Mega Stores, Chikitsalayas (CK), Arogya Kendras (AK) and Grameen Arogya Kendras (GAK), this expanding portfolio enables us to make relevant, accessible products available to households across urban and rural Bharat.
At Patanjali Foods, our relationship with Bharat’s households has grown around the everyday choices that shape how people eat, live and care. Edible oils, staples, biscuits, soya foods and nutrition have long given us a place in kitchens and on dining tables across the country. Today, that relationship reaches much further.

FY 2025-26 marked the first full year of the Home and Personal Care business within Patanjali Foods, extending our consumer presence from nourishment to everyday care. Established brands such as Dant Kanti, Kesh Kanti, Saundarya and others now sit alongside our food and nutrition portfolio, taking us into more parts of the home and more moments of daily life.
This expansion represents more than the addition of new categories. It is shaping a broader, stronger FMCG platform, bringing food, nutrition, personal care and home care together within one consumer portfolio. It allows us to serve households across a wider spectrum of needs, life stages, aspirations and price points, while building on our longstanding association with health, wellness and Ayurveda.
Strategically, this is also advancing our transition towards a contemporary FMCG-led consumer company. The growing contribution of consumer businesses supports our stated direction of moving towards a more balanced 50:50 revenue mix between FMCG and Edible Oils. In FY 2025-26, FMCG accounted for 27.60% of revenue from operations and 61.13% of total EBITDA, reflecting its increasing significance within our overall business mix.

Nourishing Bharat by bringing everyday choices closer to where people live, shop and consume.
For a country as large and diverse as Bharat, access is as important as choice. We are taking our portfolio closer to consumers by building reach across geographies, retail formats and digital channels.
Our distribution architecture connects traditional trade, Patanjali franchise stores comprising Mega Stores, Chikitsalayas, Arogya Kendras and Grameen Arogya Kendras, modern retail and emerging digital platforms. With more than 2 Million retail touchpoints and over 8,000 distributors across the country, this network gives us the scale to serve consumers across urban centres, smaller towns and rural markets.

Growing More of Bharat’s Needs at Home
Nourishing Bharat by strengthening the domestic foundations of its edible oil needs.
India’s journey towards greater self-reliance in edible oils requires stronger domestic capacity. Patanjali Foods is helping build it through an expanding, integrated oil palm ecosystem rooted in Bharat.

During FY 2025-26, our planted area under oil palm cultivation expanded to 1,10,722 hectares across 12 States. Supported by six oil mills with an aggregate capacity of 1.15 Mn MTs, our ecosystem spans the value chain from seedlings and cultivation to procurement and processing. Commercial production also commenced at our oil palm mill in Arunachal Pradesh, further strengthening our integrated domestic sourcing and processing ecosystem.
Imports met 56.00% of India’s edible oil consumption in 2024-25, underscoring the country’s continued dependence on global markets. Strengthening domestic production is therefore important not only for food security, but also for reducing exposure to global price and supply volatility.

Our oil palm programme is aligned with the National Mission on Edible Oils – Oil Palm (NMEO-OP) and the broader Aatmanirbhar Bharat vision. By expanding domestic cultivation and linking it more closely with procurement and processing, we are strengthening backward integration while helping build a more resilient edible oil value chain.

The impact is already tangible. Procurement from domestic oil palm plantations contributed to approximately 10.9% import substitution during the year, reducing reliance on imported raw materials and strengthening supply chain resilience. For Bharat, this means greater domestic capacity and steady progress towards a more self-reliant edible oil ecosystem.

About Patanjali Foods
As one of India’s leading diversified consumer companies, Patanjali Foods brings together everyday consumption, health, wellness and self-reliance.

As one of India’s leading diversified consumer companies, Patanjali Foods brings together everyday consumption, health, wellness and self-reliance.
Rooted in Indian traditions of well-being and guided by contemporary innovation, we seek to make healthier and happier choices accessible to more households. Across edible oils, food and nutrition, home and personal care and renewable energy, we serve consumers through brands that are accessible and trusted. Our capabilities in manufacturing, procurement and distribution enable us to play a meaningful role in Bharat’s evolving consumption story.
Over the past few years, we have transformed from an edible oil-led business into a broader FMCG enterprise. The integration of food, home, and personal care has expanded our relevance to consumers and strengthened our business mix. Alongside this, our growing oil palm operations are deepening the domestic edible oils value chain, supporting local production and building greater resilience against global supply and price volatility.

We are committed to growing responsibly and creating lasting value. Our approach combines respect for time-tested practices with a continued focus on innovation, resource efficiency and responsible sourcing. We are increasing the contribution of renewable energy and supporting the farmers and communities linked to our operations. Strong governance, ethical conduct and transparent reporting underpin these efforts, helping us build trust and contribute to a healthier and more sustainable Bharat.

Message to our Stakeholders
Dear Stakeholders,

Dear Stakeholders,
We are pleased to share with you an overview of FY 2025-26, a pivotal year in Patanjali Foods’ journey of growth and value creation. Amid a volatile external environment, the Company continued to script a bigger and better consumption story for India, with enhanced focus on innovation and distribution. The complete integration of the Home and Personal Care (HPC) segment into the FMCG business has unlocked new opportunities for expansion and growth. It has strengthened our FMCG proposition and elevated brand Patanjali Foods as the preferred choice of Bharat for natural, healthy and Ayurveda-based products rooted in premium quality and affordability, and resonating with the deepest consumer aspirations and expectations.
In a year of continuing transition and more efficient execution, we delivered our highest-ever annual revenue, crossing the `40,000 Crore milestone for the first time."

Robust fundamentals driving growth

Robust fundamentals driving growth
In a year of continuing transition and more efficient execution, we delivered our highest-ever annual revenue, crossing the `40,000 Crore milestone for the first time. This performance, backed by healthy double-digit growth across the edible oil and FMCG segments, has further strengthened our position as one of India’s fastest- growing FMCG Company. A sharp, sustained focus on scaling our operational and financial efficiencies enabled us to continue delivering long-term value for our stakeholders. We further expanded the ambit of our backward integration into the oil palm plantation business to nurture India’s need for self-sufficiency in edible oil, rewriting the industry landscape with our forward-looking vision and pioneering initiatives.

Strengthening self- sufficiency in edible oils

Strengthening self- sufficiency in edible oils
The Indian edible oil market, which is a pivot for household kitchen needs, is heavily dependent on imports, as domestic production meets only 40% of demand. The market, which reached 25.33 million tonnes in 2025, is estimated to grow to 28.34 million tonnes by 2034, but the demand-supply gap remains. The central government’s National Mission on Edible Oils – Oilseeds (NMEO-Oilseeds) aims to fill this gap by boosting production. As an active partner in this mission, Patanjali Foods is strengthening the country’s self-sufficiency in edible oils through its extensive oil palm plantation programme. This programme expanded meaningfully during the year, with the area under cultivation increasing to 1,10,722 hectares as of March 2026. Through this initiative, we are helping strengthen India’s edible oil security while creating sustainable livelihood opportunities for farmers, reducing import dependence, helping conserve valuable foreign exchange and supporting the Government’s vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat.

Operating Context
India’s consumer market is entering a broader phase of growth, supported by rising incomes, urbanisation, deeper rural participation and wider access to organised and digital retail. The domestic FMCG market is projected to grow from US$ 287.91 Billion in 2025 to US$ 1,150.21 Billion by 2034, at a CAGR of 16.64%.
Digital commerce redefines routes to market

Digital commerce redefines routes to market
Quick commerce, with delivery windows of 10-20 minutes, is resetting expectations around availability and reshaping product assortment. Faster delivery, wider choice and data-led recommendations are encouraging discovery and trial, particularly in specialised, premium and convenience-led categories. The rise of direct-to-consumer brands has also lowered entry barriers and intensified competition. With general trade remaining central to FMCG reach, the coexistence of traditional, modern and digital channels is increasing the need for channel-specific pricing, packaging, assortments, promotions and fulfilment models.
Growth is also becoming more complex. Consumers are trading up selectively while remaining value- conscious, digital channels are reshaping distribution and global volatility continues to affect input costs and supply security. These shifts favour companies with portfolio breadth, sourcing strength and the ability to serve multiple price points and channels.
Premiumisation broadens, with value still central

Policy support advances edible oil self-reliance
GST rationalisation supports affordability and formalisation
GST rationalisation has created a more supportive framework for branded consumer products. Lower rates across several food and household categories improves affordability, support volumes and encourage formal, packaged consumption. A more streamlined rate structure also reduces classification complexity. The transition required manufacturers and channel partners to revise prices, packaging and inventories. Over time, however, lower consumer prices can deepen category penetration, particularly among value-conscious households.

India’s dependence on imported edible oils exposes the sector to global production cycles, currency movements and shipping disruption. Import duties are periodically adjusted to manage domestic prices and inflation, influencing procurement, inventory and pricing decisions. Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) requirements govern food safety, quality, fortification and labelling. Alongside regulation, the National Mission on Edible Oils – Oil Palm and initiatives promoting oilseed cultivation, farmer linkages and contract farming are supporting higher domestic production and greater long-term self-reliance.

Risk Management
At Patanjali Foods, proactive risk management helps us navigate volatility across markets, supply chains and technologies while protecting continuity, stakeholder interests and long-term value.
Identifying and Assessing Risk
We follow a structured and forward-looking process to identify and assess risks across our operations and value chain. Periodic assessments combine qualitative judgement with quantitative analysis, enabling us to understand the likelihood, potential impact and interdependencies of identified risks. Risk assessments are integrated into business planning and operational reviews and draw upon multiple internal and external inputs.

The evolving macroeconomic landscape, geopolitical developments, regulatory changes, technological advancements and climate-related considerations continue to shape our operating environment. Recognising these uncertainties, we embed risk management within strategic planning and decision-making to strengthen organisational resilience, safeguard stakeholder interests and support sustainable growth.

Testing provides the evidence that supports our quality systems. Manufacturing locations maintain chemical, microbiology and packaging laboratories operated by trained and qualified personnel.
Our responsibility for quality continues after products enter the market. Finished products are sampled on an ongoing basis across India to assess product quality, packaging integrity and other relevant parameters.

Our responsibility for quality continues after products enter the market. Finished products are sampled on an ongoing basis across India to assess product quality, packaging integrity and other relevant parameters.
Consistent quality is supported by a structured governance framework that extends across sourcing, manufacturing and product release. Supplier qualification, internal audits and risk assessments are complemented by clearly established specifications and standard operating procedures for raw materials, packaging materials, process chemicals and finished goods. Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) mechanisms further support the timely identification and resolution of quality-related issues.
Our laboratories use analytical instruments including GC, HPLC, PCR, NIR, UV-Vis, NMR, Soxhlet and Tintometer to support testing across relevant quality parameters. Incoming materials are inspected before approval, while finished products undergo batch-release testing. Round-robin testing is also undertaken to support analytical reliability and consistency between plants.

Insights from market sampling are complemented by continuous monitoring of customer complaints, customer satisfaction (CSAT) and customer dissatisfaction (DSAT) scores and broader market feedback. This helps identify potential issues at the consumer end and creates an additional feedback mechanism for improving product quality, packaging and overall product delivery.

Two genuinely owned climate assets

Two genuinely owned climate assets
The visibility across value chain emissions, spanning agricultural raw materials, third-party logistics and purchased goods, is still being progressively built to establish a complete, auditable Scope 3 baseline for a credible net- zero commitment. Committing to net zero ahead of this maturity would risk an unsubstantiated pledge rather than a verifiable one.
Only a few companies within the edible oils or FMCG sector simultaneously operate a utility- scale renewable energy portfolio and a large, mature and nature-based carbon sink. This combination allows Patanjali Foods to make near- term and verifiable neutrality claims grounded within its own physical assets’ operations, rather than externally purchased carbon credits or offsets of variable quality.
Carbon Neutrality First in the coming years, Net Zero on the Horizon

Our 1,10,722 ha oil palm plantation network serves as a significant nature-based climate asset. As perennial palms grow, they continuously accumulate biomass, capturing and storing atmospheric carbon throughout their growth cycle.
The Science Behind
Unlike annual or seasonal crops, which store carbon and release it back into the atmosphere during harvest, oil palm is a long-lived perennial plantation that typically remains in production for 25 to 30 years. Across this growth cycle, the palm continuously accumulates biomass both above ground (trunk, fronds and canopies) and below ground (root systems). As the plantation matures, these living carbon sinks continue to capture and store atmospheric carbon, contributing to the Company's climate mitigation efforts through biological carbon sequestration, and complementing the emissions avoided through our renewable energy portfolio.
The rate of carbon accumulation is closely tied to the plantation's age profile. Biomass and carbon storage accrue most rapidly during the young-to-prime growth phase and broadly during the 4th to 25th year of a palm's life before tapering as the tree reaches full maturity.

Management Discussion and Analysis
Global Economy
The world economy maintained stability throughout 2025 by handling shifting trade rules and mixed results across regions. Heavy investments in technology offset the impact of fresh tariffs and changing government policies. Global inflation settled at a manageable 4.1% as many countries delivered numbers below what markets first predicted.

Household spending increased steadily across the world in 2025, driven by tech spending and higher wages in major areas. Consumers in the United States and emerging Asian countries spent more on goods and services as financial conditions improved. This stronger demand helped soften the blow from tariff pressures. Global job markets were resilient in 2025 despite trade disruptions and policy uncertainty. Technology and services sectors added jobs steadily while manufacturing growth slowed. Reliable employment levels supported rising household incomes and broader economic strength.
Outlook
Emerging markets maintain strong momentum at 3.8% growth. China projects 4.6% expansion in 2026 backed by domestic stimulus and improved US trade relations. India continues as a leading performer with 6.4% growth, positioning as a global hub for manufacturing and digital transformation.
The global economy moves toward steady growth projected at 3.0% for 2026 before easing slightly to 3.4% in 2027. Technology-led productivity gains, particularly from artificial intelligence spreading into industry and medicine, drive this progress. These advances help offset ongoing trade tensions and shifting political landscapes.

The geopolitical environment remains uncertain, with escalating tensions in West Asia emerging as a key risk for global trade, energy flows and supply chains. Recent developments in the region have increased concerns around the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global energy shipments, while also contributing to higher crude oil prices, tighter LNG availability and broader market volatility. At the same time, the Russia-Ukraine conflict continues to affect oil supply, commodity prices and logistics, adding to the pressure on global markets. These developments are likely to create indirect challenges across sectors through higher input costs, shipment delays and uncertainty in the availability of essential materials and services.
Global headline inflation increases gradually to 4.7% in 2026 and further declines to 3.9% in 2027. Advanced economies approach inflation targets more slowly, particularly in the United States. Central banks adjust policy rates carefully, with gradual cuts in the United States and the United Kingdom, steady rates in the euro area and modest increases in Japan. World trade growth moderates to 3.5% in 2026 due to tariff adjustments, though technology exports continue providing essential support.

Advanced economies should expand by 1.7% in 2026. The United States leads this group with expected 2.3% growth supported by tax incentives under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Market recovery after the short 2025 federal shutdown creates ideal conditions for private investment and consumer spending. The euro area moderates at 0.9%, serving as a reliable global anchor. Japan recalibrates to 0.6% growth following recent policy adjustments.
World GDP expanded by 3.5% in 2025, showing varied speeds across regions. Advanced economies achieved 1.9% growth, with the United States reaching 2.1% through technology investments and policy backing. The euro area recorded 1.4% while Japan managed 1.1%. Emerging markets outperformed with 4.5% overall growth led by India's strong 7.7% expansion and China's steady 5.0% rise.

Industry Overview
Staple Food Market
India's staple food market is undergoing a gradual shift from loose and unbranded products towards branded and packaged offerings, supported by changing consumer preferences, wider organised retail access and the expansion of digital commerce. The India staple food market was valued at $57.93 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $85.72 billion by 2031, registering a CAGR of 6.93% during 2026-31. Grains and cereals accounted for 44.71% of the market in 2025, supported by the continued importance of rice and wheat in household and institutional consumption.

Product innovation is creating additional opportunities within the category, particularly through fortification, premiumisation and functional variants. Flours such as atta, maida and rice flour are seeing greater adoption of multigrain and high-protein variants, while millet-based and value-added products are gaining visibility. Pulses and legumes are expected to be the fastest-growing product category, with a projected CAGR of 7.96% through 2031, supported by increasing protein awareness and dietary diversification among urban consumers.
Indian FMCG Market
The Indian FMCG market reached $287.91 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow to $1,150.21 billion by 2034, exhibiting a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 16.64% during 2026- 2034. This strong expansion reflects higher disposable incomes, rapid urbanisation, and greater consumer focus on branded goods. Personal care and cosmetics lead with 48% market share in 2025, driven by demand for skincare, hygiene products, and grooming essentials across all age groups.

India's FMCG market has established itself as the epicentre of consumer spending, encompassing everyday essentials like personal care products, packaged foods, household goods, and over-the- counter medicines that reach households across urban and rural areas. This sector thrives on high-volume sales through kirana stores, supermarkets, and growing e-commerce platforms, serving a diverse population with both branded and value offerings. Rising incomes and changing lifestyles have shifted demand towards convenience and premium products, making FMCG a resilient segment even during economic fluctuations.
The shift towards packaged staples is being supported by greater consumer preference for hygiene, consistent quality, traceability and convenience. Organised retail, e-commerce and quick commerce are further improving accessibility and assortment across categories such as rice, wheat flour, pulses, edible oils and millets. The expansion of these channels is also providing branded players with greater opportunities to increase product visibility and introduce differentiated offerings.

The industry, however, remains exposed to agricultural supply conditions and commodity price movements. Dependence on monsoon patterns can affect the availability and cost of key raw materials, while post-harvest losses and intermediary-driven procurement channels can add to supply-chain inefficiencies. These factors can create volatility in input costs and place pressure on margins for processors and branded packaged food companies.

The increasing adoption of chocolates and other contemporary confectionery products alongside traditional sweets is creating additional consumption occasions, while e-commerce and quick commerce are making products more accessible, particularly during periods of heightened seasonal demand.

Indian Biscuit and Confectionery Market
The Indian confectionery market continues to expand, supported by rising disposable incomes, urbanisation and changing consumer preferences towards indulgent and convenient products. The market was valued at ₹398.71 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach ₹618.10 billion by 2034, registering a CAGR of 4.99% during 2026–34. The category continues to benefit from India's strong cultural association with sweets and gifting, while modern retail and e-commerce are improving product availability across urban and semi-urban markets.
Indian Biscuits Market

Indian Biscuits Market
The Indian biscuits market is evolving with changing consumption patterns, rising preference for convenient snacking and increasing consumer awareness around nutrition. The market was valued at $5.0 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $8.5 billion by 2034, registering a CAGR of 5.70% during 2026-34. The market is supported by demand across urban and rural markets, with product innovation and wider distribution helping manufacturers cater to changing consumer preferences.
The industry, however, remains exposed to rising health concerns around sugar consumption, volatility in the prices of key inputs such as sugar, cocoa and palm oil, and intense competition across organised and unorganised players. Maintaining product quality and freshness across India's varied climatic conditions also requires efficient logistics and supply-chain capabilities. Going forward, product innovation, premiumisation, healthier formulations and wider distribution across modern and digital retail channels are expected to remain important to the growth of India's confectionery market.

India's soy protein supply chain remains closely linked to domestic soybean production and processing capacity. India's soy-processing system has an installed crushing capacity of approximately 11.4 million tonnes. Fluctuations in soybean availability and crushing economics can, however, affect capacity utilisation and input costs, making procurement and proximity to soybean-producing regions important factors for processors.
Consumer preferences are also broadening beyond traditional confectionery towards premium and differentiated offerings. Chocolate accounted for 36.5% of the market in 2025, supported by increasing preference for premium treats, gifting and new flavour combinations. Manufacturers are introducing products that combine local flavours such as cardamom, jaggery and masala chai with contemporary confectionery formats, while premium packaging and limited-edition products are supporting consumption across gifting and celebratory occasions.

Health and nutrition are becoming important considerations in biscuit consumption. Consumers are increasingly seeking products made with whole grains and ingredients such as oats and millets, while demand is also emerging for gluten-free, sugar-free, low- calorie and fortified variants. This is encouraging manufacturers to develop products positioned around fibre, digestive health, immunity and overall wellbeing, particularly among health-conscious urban consumers.
The market also faces increasing competition from alternative protein sources, including pea, dairy and wheat proteins. Raw-material price volatility and the availability of alternative plant-based proteins can influence demand and margins, while processors need to maintain product quality and develop application-specific capabilities to differentiate their offerings.
Indian Soya Protein Market
India's soya protein market is expanding with increasing demand for plant-based protein across food and beverage, nutritional supplements and other applications. The market was valued at $570 million in 2025 and is projected to reach $795 million by 2031, registering a CAGR of 5.65% during 2026-31, compared with a historical CAGR of 5.13% during 2020-25. The market's growth is being supported by wider use of soy protein in bakery products, beverages, meal replacements, protein powders and affordable meat substitutes.

At the same time, the category is witnessing premiumisation, with consumers showing greater interest in differentiated flavours, higher-quality ingredients and indulgent products. Rising disposable incomes and changing lifestyles are supporting demand for premium biscuits and cookies, while manufacturers are introducing variants using ingredients such as dark chocolate, nuts and dried fruits to broaden the consumption occasion.
Health and wellness considerations are influencing product development within the category. Growing awareness of sugar consumption is increasing demand for sugar-free, low-calorie and functional confectionery products. Manufacturers are responding through reduced-sugar formulations and the use of natural sweeteners such as stevia and jaggery, creating opportunities for products that combine indulgence with changing consumer preferences.
Going forward, the continued adoption of plant-based protein, expansion of functional foods and nutritional supplements, and wider applications of textured and higher-purity soy proteins are expected to support the growth of India's soy protein market. The ability to secure soybean supplies, maintain consistent product quality and cater to evolving food and nutrition applications will remain important for participants across the value chain.

Convenience remains another important demand driver. Busy lifestyles are increasing the preference for portable and easy-to- consume snacks, supporting the adoption of single-pouch, resealable and travel-friendly packs. The expansion of e-commerce is further improving access to a wider range of packaged biscuit products, while supermarkets, hypermarkets and convenience stores continue to provide important distribution channels.
Food and beverage applications accounted for 48.63% of demand in 2025, supported by the increasing use of soy protein in plant-based foods and other protein-enriched products. Nutritional supplements are expected to be among the faster-growing applications, supported by increasing consumer interest in protein-rich diets, sports nutrition and health-oriented products. Business Segments
Patanjali Foods operates across three principal business segments — FMCG, Edible Oils and Wind Turbine Power Generation. The FMCG portfolio spans food, biscuits, textured soya protein, nutraceuticals and home & personal care, while the Edible Oils business covers edible oil refining and seed crushing, branded and bulk edible oils, oil palm plantations and related downstream opportunities. Patanjali Foods Limited (referred to as ‘Patanjali’ or the Company) is a diversified consumer and food-processing company with businesses spanning FMCG, edible oils and wind turbine power generation. The Company traces its origins to 1986 and has evolved from its traditional edible oils and soya processing operations into a broader consumer platform comprising food, biscuits, textured soya protein, nutraceuticals and home & personal care. Its business model combines consumer brands and distribution capabilities with a broad manufacturing base and participation across upstream and downstream stages of the edible oils value chain.

Patanjali operates a geographically distributed manufacturing network comprising 26 manufacturing locations across India. The footprint extends across locations including Kandla, Mangalore, Kakinada, Chennai, Haldia, Patalganga, Nagpur, Guna, Gadarwara, Peddapuram, Jammu, Haridwar, Newasa and Niglok, providing manufacturing capabilities across its principal businesses.

The Company’s financial risk management framework covers exposures arising from commodity price fluctuations, foreign currency movements and interest rate variations. These exposures are managed under Board-approved Foreign Exchange Risk Management and Commodity Price Risk Management Policies and supported by a prudent hedging framework. Foreign currency exposures relating to imports and exports are managed through forward and futures contracts, while commodity price risks are mitigated through futures contracts, sale contracts and mutually agreed supply arrangements. As part of our commitment to transparency, accountability, and respect for human rights, we have established internal mechanisms to identify, receive, and address grievances related to human rights concerns. Employees and workers can raise concerns through multiple accessible channels, including HR Konnect, the Prevention of Sexual Harassment (PoSH) Committee, and dedicated email channels, with options for direct or anonymous reporting. The Code of Conduct and Whistleblower Policy also provide mechanisms for reporting concerns, including potential human rights violations, without fear of retaliation.
All complaints are handled with due consideration to fairness, confidentiality, non-retaliation, and procedural integrity. These mechanisms support a transparent and accountable workplace culture while protecting complainants from adverse treatment for raising concerns in good faith.
9. Do human rights requirements form part of your business agreements and contracts?

9. Do human rights requirements form part of your business agreements and contracts?
Yes, human rights requirements are incorporated into our business agreements and contractual relationships, as guided by our Human Rights Policy. The policy extends beyond employees to cover key stakeholders, including associates, customers, vendors, and contractors, thereby supporting the integration of human rights principles across our business and supply chain.
Our grievance redressal mechanisms extend beyond employees to cover suppliers, farmers, local communities, and other stakeholders who may be impacted by our business activities. Site-level grievance channels and community engagement programmes provide avenues for external stakeholders to raise concerns and seek appropriate resolution.
Our commitments include equal opportunity, non-discrimination, prevention of harassment, diversity and inclusion, and the prohibition of child and forced labour. We also respect the rights to freedom of association, opinion, and expression, while promoting fair wages, safe working conditions, and a healthy workplace. By extending these principles to vendors and contractors, we reinforce responsible business practices and ensure that respect for human rights forms an integral part of our contractual and business relationships.

We give particular attention to vulnerable and marginalized groups, including women, children, migrant workers, and marginalized communities. Grievance channels are designed to be accessible, confidential, and sensitive to local contexts, including the provision for grievances to be raised in local languages where required.
All grievances received are formally documented, reviewed, and investigated by the HR function, under the oversight of the Chief Operating Officer (COO). Appropriate corrective actions are taken based on the findings, and outcomes are communicated to the concerned parties, subject to confidentiality and anonymity requirements.

The Company, as a lessee, recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for its leasing arrangements, if the contract conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset. A contract is, or contains, a lease if the contract conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration. The contract conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset, if it involves the use of an identified asset and the Company has substantially all of the economic benefits from use of the asset through the period of the lease and has right to direct the use of the identified asset. The cost of the right-of-use asset shall comprise of the amount of the initial measurement of the lease liability adjusted for any lease payments made at or before the commencement date plus any initial direct costs incurred. The right-of-use assets is subsequently measured at cost less any accumulated depreciation, accumulated impairment losses, if any and adjusted for any remeasurement of the lease liability. The right-of-use assets is depreciated using the straight-line method from the commencement date over the shorter of lease term and useful life of right-of-use asset. The Company measures the lease liability at the present value of the lease payments that are not paid at the commencement date of the lease. The lease payments are discounted using the interest rate implicit in the lease, if that rate can be readily determined. If that rate cannot be readily determined, the Company uses incremental borrowing rate. For short-term and low value leases, the Company recognises the lease payments as an operating expense on a straight-line basis over the lease term. Lease

Liquidity risk is the risk that the Company will not be able to meet its financial obligations as they become due. The Company has been taking measures to ensure that the Company’s cash flow from business borrowing is sufficient to meet the cash requirements for the Company’s operations. The Company managing its liquidity needs by monitoring forecasted cash inflows and outflows in day to day business. Liquidity needs are monitored on various time bands, on a day to day and week to week basis, as well as on the basis of a rolling 30 day projections. Net cash requirements are compared to available working capital facilities in order to determine headroom or any short falls. Presently company’s objective is to maintain sufficient cash to meet its operational liquidity requirements.

6. A company’s internal financial controls with reference to consolidated financial statements is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of consolidated financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company’s internal financial controls with reference to consolidated financial statements include those policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of consolidated financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorisations of management and directors of the company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of the company’s assets that could have a material effect on the consolidated financial statements.

When the Group has transferred its rights to receive cash flows from an asset or has entered into a pass-through arrangement, it evaluates if and to what extent it has retained the risks and rewards of ownership. When it has neither transferred nor retained substantially all of the risks and rewards of the asset, nor transferred control of the asset, the Group continues to recognise the transferred asset to the extent of the Group’s continuing involvement. The Group, as a lessee, recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for its leasing arrangements, if the contract conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset. A contract is, or contains, a lease if the contract conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration. The contract conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset, if it involves the use of an identified asset and the Company has substantially all of the economic benefits from use of the asset through the period of the lease and has right to direct the use of the identified asset. The cost of the right-of-use asset shall comprise of the amount of the initial measurement of the lease liability adjusted for any lease payments made at or before the commencement date plus any initial direct costs incurred. The right-of-use assets is subsequently measured at cost less any accumulated depreciation, accumulated impairment losses, if any and adjusted for any remeasurement of the lease liability. The right-of-use assets is depreciated using the straight-line method from the commencement date over the shorter of lease term and useful life of right-of-use asset. The Group measures the lease liability at the present value of the lease payments that are not paid at the commencement date of the lease. The lease payments are discounted using the interest rate implicit in the lease, if that rate can be readily determined. If that rate cannot be readily determined, the Group uses incremental borrowing rate. For short-term and low value leases, the Group recognises the lease payments as an operating expense on a straight- line basis over the lease term.

Lease liability is subsequently remeasured by increasing the carrying amount to reflect interest on the lease liability and reducing the carrying amount to reflect the lease payments made.

Under the Supplier Bills Discounting, the Group enters into supplier finance arrangements with various finance providers to facilitate the early payment of dues on its behalf to the Group’s vendors who may elect to factor their invoice through such financial institutions. The finance providers pay the amounts to a participating vendor in respect of invoices owed by the Group and receive settlement from the Group at a later date. By virtue of commercial agreements with the vendors, the Group remains obligated to settle invoices at the contractually agreed payment terms and is not impacted by the decision of vendor to obtain early financing from the finance providers. In this arrangement, no material extension of payment terms beyond those agreed with suppliers is offered to the Group by the finance providers. Further, the Group is not required to pledge any collateral to secure the transaction, and no fee is re-charged to the Group by the finance provider. The economic substance of the transaction is determined to be in nature of operating activity where the original contract with the vendors does not get substantially modified on entering into arrangement. Therefore, the Group has disclosed the amounts factored by vendors within trade payables because the nature and function of the liability remains the same as those of other trade payables.

a) On November 21, 2025, the Government of India notified the four Labour Codes - the Code on Wages, 2019, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the Code on Social Security, 2020, and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 - consolidating 29 existing labour laws. The Ministry of Labour & Employment published draft Central Rules and FAQs to enable assessment of the financial impact due to changes in regulations. The Group has assessed and disclosed the incremental impact of these changes based on the best information available, consistent with the guidance provided by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. Considering the materiality and regulatory-driven, non-recurring nature of this impact, the Group has presented such incremental impact as Exceptional Items in the statement of profit and loss for the year ended March 31, 2026. The incremental impact costing of gratuity of ₹ 1,655.07 lakh and compensated absences of ₹ 1,364.02 lakh primarily arises due to change in wage definition. during this conference call, please signal an operator by pressing star then zero on your touchtone
phone. Please note that this conference is being recorded.
I now hand the conference over to Mr. Sanjeev Asthana, CEO, Patanjali Foods. Thank you, and
over to you, sir.
Sanjeev Asthana: Thank you, and good morning to everyone joining us today. A warm welcome to all of you on
Patanjali Foods Limited's call to discuss the financial performance for Q1 FY27. I am
accompanied by the company's CFO, Kumar Rajeshji, along with Mr. Priyendu Jha from
Investor Relations and our IR partners, Strategic Growth Advisors. The results collateral has
been uploaded on the stock exchanges as well as on the company's website for your reference.
Let me now take you through a quick snapshot of our financial performance for the quarter.
During the course of the call, we will be referring to the standalone financials. We continued to
build on this momentum, delivering our fourth consecutive quarter of highest-ever quarterly
revenues supported by healthy growth in profitability.
Specifically, revenue from operations stood at INR11,337 crores, growing 29% year-on-year.
Operating EBITDA for the period was INR543 crores with a margin at 4.80%, while profit
before tax stood at INR453 crores, translating into PBT margin of 4%.

chunks.section: Aug 2026 earnings call · Q1 FY2027 · Ramji Lal Gupta
chunks.text:
before tax stood at INR453 crores, translating into PBT margin of 4%.
Turning to the segmental performance now, our edible oil segment delivered quarterly revenue
of INR8,505 crores, marking the highest-ever quarterly revenue with growth led primarily by
the mustard oil. Quarterly EBITDA margin came in at 5.22%. On the oil palm plantation front,
the company generated highest-ever quarterly revenue of INR740 crores in Q1 FY27. Revenues
grew by 25% year-on-year.
This growth is closely aligned with the Government of India's National Mission on Edible Oils
- Oil Palm, which has strengthened farmer viability pricing and planting assistance to drive India
towards self-reliance in edible oils. As of 30th June '26, the cultivated area stood at 1,15,861
hectares with nearly 37% of the area in the prime yielding phase of 7 to 25 years, against total
allocated area of 6.63 lakh hectares.
Turning now to our FMCG segment, the quarterly revenue stood at INR2,938 crores with
EBITDA of INR190 crores and EBITDA margin of 6.45% in Q1 FY27. The segment contributed
nearly 26% of revenues and nearly 30% of EBITDA, excluding unallocable income during the
quarter. Within FMCG by category, the biscuits generated revenue of INR560 crores, registering
Page 2 of 13
Patanjali Foods Limited August 17, 2026
year-on-year growth of 27%, reflecting continued consumer trust and preference, with EBITDA

chunks.section: Aug 2026 earnings call · Q1 FY2027 · Ramji Lal Gupta
chunks.text:
year-on-year growth of 27%, reflecting continued consumer trust and preference, with EBITDA
margin of 15.35% versus 9.35% in the same period last year.
Revenue from consumer staples segment stood at more than INR1,000 crores in Q1 FY27. A
confluence of weather and geopolitical factors are expected to create some challenges here, but
healthy government grain inventories and timely policy intervention should help mitigate the
impact.
The textured soya product division recorded revenue of INR160 crores in Q1 FY27, growing
14% year-on-year and 50% quarter-on-quarter with EBITDA margin of over 18%. Our beverage
portfolio generated revenue of INR38 crores, driven by extended summers aided by delayed
onset of monsoon, as well as new product launches including mango chutney, mango panna
juice, and orange juice.
Ghee sales were softer during the quarter and generated revenue of INR219 crores, reflecting
the seasonal nature of demand and lower summer off-take in export-oriented markets,
particularly in the Middle East, where geopolitical tensions disrupted normal consumption and
trade patterns.
Our other food categories including honey, dry fruits, spices and condiments, herbal products,
etc, collectively generated revenues of INR203 crores during the quarter. Revenue from
nutraceuticals stood at INR18 crores with sports nutrition gaining significant momentum. Our

chunks.section: Aug 2026 earnings call · Q1 FY2027 · Ramji Lal Gupta
chunks.text:
nutraceuticals stood at INR18 crores with sports nutrition gaining significant momentum. Our
Home and Personal Care business delivered a strong performance with a total revenue of
INR629 crores in Q1 FY27.
Within the category, the skin care emerged as a major revenue growth driver and dental care
inched up on EBITDA and EBITDA margin side. The dental care segment generated revenues
of INR325 crores, followed by skin care at INR165 crores. Home care revenue stood at INR83
crores, while hair care and other products generated INR56 crores.
Let me now give you a brief overview of the operating environment. With a combination of
delayed monsoon and West Asia conflict, we saw commodity price inflation in Q1. This cuts
both ways for us. On one hand, we carry long positions in edible oils, so the resulting commodity
price inflation has actually been a net positive for the business.
On the other, the same inflation raises input costs for several of our FMCG businesses, weighing
on their profitability. Net-net, the impact on Patanjali as a whole is smaller than it would be for
a pure-play FMCG company, though we are operating in a challenging environment through this
quarter and into the next.
In edible oils, we had witnessed substantial drop, in veg oil, EBITDA last year; This, year,
however, we are seeing inflation returning in volatile veg oil markets, driven largely by

chunks.section: Aug 2026 earnings call · Q1 FY2027 · Ramji Lal Gupta
chunks.text:
however, we are seeing inflation returning in volatile veg oil markets, driven largely by
petroleum prices and genuine supply shortages across the spectrum.
This is working in our favor, offsetting much of the input cost pressure elsewhere in the portfolio
and keeps us on course to deliver both the growth and the overall margin construct we have
Page 3 of 13
Patanjali Foods Limited August 17, 2026
guided to for the company, even after accounting for the raw material inflation flowing through
from delayed monsoon.
In this dynamic environment, we remain agile on pricing as input costs evolve. We took
calibrated price increases in the edible oil segment while using targeted discounts in our FMCG
portfolio to remain competitive. We also introduced smaller pack sizes to address changing
consumer needs and market requirements.
This calibrated approach to pricing and pack architecture, helped us navigate the environment
effectively. Such pricing measures are continuing in the current quarter as well as across the
industry. Despite some delay in the monsoon, recent data on sowing of Kharif, including rice,
pulses, coarse cereals, sugarcane, etc, has showcased resilience.Acreage gap has narrowed to
1.9% vis-à-vis last year. In fact, oilseeds saw a rise in area, which is expected to get further boost
with widespread rainfall across key growing regions.

chunks.section: Aug 2026 earnings call · Q1 FY2027 · Ramji Lal Gupta
chunks.text:
with widespread rainfall across key growing regions.
On the input front, the palm oil prices has begun firming in March 2026, remained positive
following the onset of the war, but turned marginally lower after de-escalation in the latter part
of the quarter.
Futures factored in the same and prices turned lower. Still, domestic prices were supported by
rupee depreciation of 2.5% and again by festival period palm oil prices reached 2-week high in
mid-August. The soya oil price futures increased by 40% towards the end of March and then
stabilized towards the end of June, the FOB prices corrected by 6% amidst lower demand,
leading to a sharper decline in physical prices with further firming similar to palm oil price trend.
In the current environment, physical-oriented hedging strategy rather than reliance on futures
alone, along with timely import purchases, helped us in capturing divergence and improve the
margins. Wheat prices have remained largely stable during the quarter, while milk prices trended
upwards on the back of higher procurement costs. Sugar prices, too, stayed firm amidst lower
domestic production and tighter inventory levels.
Certain Home and Personal Care products continue to face elevated input cost pressures. In
addition to all this, we saw an increase in packaging, freight, and logistics costs during the

chunks.section: Aug 2026 earnings call · Q1 FY2027 · Ramji Lal Gupta
chunks.text:
addition to all this, we saw an increase in packaging, freight, and logistics costs during the
quarter. Let me now move on to some of the other key business updates for the quarter. I want
to take a moment to share some updates on our team.
Our CFO, Kumar Rajesh, was honored with the Best CFO of the Year award at the Asia Business
Leader of the Year Awards. On behalf of the entire team, I want to congratulate him on this well-
deserved honor.
During the quarter, we launched several new products including Rose Kanti soap, Dant Kanti
Sensitive toothpaste, Super Dishwash liquid, Sweet Lime pickle, Almond and Chyawanprash
cookies, in addition to our summer-focused launches.
We have also rolled out a range of new Dant Kanti variants that are performing exceedingly
well. We are increasingly micro-segmenting this portfolio by population, by choice architecture,
Page 4 of 13
Patanjali Foods Limited August 17, 2026
and specifically to address the Gen Z requirements for the toothpaste. The staples category is
expected to see the most rural stress-related pressure this quarter, while Home and Personal Care
overall should continue to grow well.
On the distribution front, we continue to strengthen our presence across e-commerce and quick

chunks.section: Jun 2026 earnings call · Q4 FY2026 · Ramji Lal Gupta
chunks.text:
very warm welcome to Patanjali Foods Limited's call to discuss the financial performance for
Q4 '26 and FY '26. I'm accompanied by the company's CFO, Kumar Rajesh ji, along with Mr.
Priyendu Jha from the Investor Relations team, and our Investor Relations partner, Strategic
Growth Advisors. We have uploaded the results collateral on the stock exchanges as well as the
company's website for your reference.
Let me begin with a quick snapshot of our financial performance. During the call, we will be
referring to the standalone financials. FY'26 is our first full year after the integration of the HPC
business, and we saw progressive momentum in each quarter. At the company level, we crossed
the INR40,000 crore mark in the top line terms. This performance was backed by healthy double-
digit growth across the edible oil and FMCG segments.
Revenue from operations stood at INR40,169 (to be read as 40,169.58) crores during the period.
Total EBITDA excluding the exceptional items for the period was INR1,931 (to be read as
1,931.52) crores with a margin of 4.79%, and the profit before taxes stood at INR1,353 (to be
read as 1,353.94) crores translating into PBT margin of approximately 3.36%.
In Q4 of '26, the company delivered the highest ever quarterly revenue from operations
amounting to INR11,155 (to be read as 11,155.60) crores, total EBITDA excluding exceptional

chunks.section: Jun 2026 earnings call · Q4 FY2026 · Ramji Lal Gupta
chunks.text:
amounting to INR11,155 (to be read as 11,155.60) crores, total EBITDA excluding exceptional
items for the period was INR501.96 crores with a margin of 4.48% and profit before tax stood
at INR235.69 crores, translating into a PBT margin of approximately 2.10%.
Let me now give a brief overview of the operating environment for Q4 '26.
On the demand front, the domestic demand trends remain resilient and structurally healthy
during the quarter. Consumption was supported by improved channel offtakes following
normalization after the GST transition.
Both urban and rural markets contributed to demand recovery. Urban demand benefited from
recent tax relief measures, while the rural demand remained supported by a healthy crop season
and continued government welfare spending. The retail inflation largely remained under control
at 3.4% in March '26 versus 3.21% in Feb of 2026.
Page 2 of 12
Patanjali Foods Limited May 30, 2026
On the input cost front, the edible oil complex witnessed a sharp price increase in March '26,
primarily due to the crude oil volatility amid ongoing geopolitical uncertainties. RBD palm,
refined wheat and deodorized palm oil prices increased by 20% (Note: It is an approximate
number) between Jan and March '26, driven by tighter supply expectations, firm demand,
Indonesia's proposal for B45 biodiesel program, and lower CPO production in Malaysia.

chunks.section: Jun 2026 earnings call · Q4 FY2026 · Ramji Lal Gupta
chunks.text:
Indonesia's proposal for B45 biodiesel program, and lower CPO production in Malaysia.
The refined soy oil prices also moved higher, increasing by 23% (Note: It is an approximate
number) during the same period, in line with global edible oil trends. Wheat and Chana prices
remained relatively stable during the quarter, supported by improved crop expectations and
higher imports, respectively. Yellow pea prices increased by 10% (Note: It is an approximate
number) during Q4 '26 due to tighter domestic supply and lower crop estimates, while sugar
prices remained broadly stable.
Across segments, the company also witnessed inflationary pressure in packaging materials,
freight and insurance costs linked to the crude oil volatility after mid-March. The cost of goods
sold increased by 98 basis points on a sequential basis. Further on, year-on-year basis, the cost
of goods sold increased by 294 basis points. The company continues to manage these pressures
through hedging initiatives, cost optimization measures and calibrated pricing actions.
Coming to April '26 and beyond due to the geopolitical tension, the prices of palm oil prices
increased by 15% and soybean and sunflower increased by 17% and 22% in April '26 on a year-
on-year basis. This has led to a noticeable shift in consumer preference towards mustard oil,
which is traditionally viewed as more expensive than palm oil.

chunks.section: Jun 2026 earnings call · Q4 FY2026 · Ramji Lal Gupta
chunks.text:
which is traditionally viewed as more expensive than palm oil.
While palm, soybean and sunflower oils largely constitute India's edible oil import basket,
mustard, groundnut and cottonseed oils are produced domestically supporting supply availability
and diversification within the edible oil basket.
Crude-linked volatility remains elevated, which would make the operating environment
increasingly challenging for smaller and unorganized players. In such a scenario, large national
brands, such as our company may be relatively better positioned to navigate the volatility,
particularly given our strong distribution network and scale advantage.
Let me now walk you through the segment-wise performance during Q4 '26. For the Edible Oil
segment, quarterly revenues stood at INR8,324 crores, registering 23.28% year-on-year growth.
EBITDA margin for the segment stood at 2.58%. Branded edible oils accounted for around 75%
of the total edible oil sales and continued to be the primary growth driver. For FY '26, the revenue
stood at INR29,313 (to be read as 29,313.54) crores, registering 18.39% year-on-year growth.
EBITDA margin for the segment stood at 2.58%. We endeavour to maintain an EBITDA in the
range of 2% to 4% for the edible oil business, despite the near-term price volatility. For the oil
palm plantation business, the government's recent advisory encouraging lower edible oil

palm plantation business, the government's recent advisory encouraging lower edible oil

palm plantation initiatives, which are focused on supporting domestic production, improved

over 12 states in India is in the prime yielding phase of 7 to 25 years. The total allocated area
stood at 6.63 lakh hectares, which was granted originally.

the revised strategic direction for the segment.

achieved a revenue of INR526 (to be read as 526.78) crores. Beverages and summer portfolio
saw encouraging momentum towards the end of the quarter with the launch of Patanjali Apple
drink. We are strengthening our presence in the fruit-based beverage category. Nutraceuticals
generated revenue of INR17.94 crores during the quarter and INR58 crores in FY26.

optimization, selective product launches, these initiatives are beginning to yield positive results.
The company remains confident in the long-term potential of India's health and wellness
segment and continues to strengthen its portfolio with launches such as Slim Choice capsules,
date almond spread and Sea Buckthorn capsules.

(to be read as 1,412.80) crores in FY26.

with annual revenues reaching INR680 crores in FY26. The Home Care revenue stood at

Guidance to the last part of my talk. Going ahead, we remain focused on strengthening our brand
portfolio, expanding our distribution footprint, driving operational efficiencies and building
scale across emerging categories. We also remain committed towards enhancing our investment
behind innovation and consumer engagement.
With our strong brand equity, integrated business model, extensive distribution network and
diversified product portfolio, we believe the company is well-positioned to navigate near-term
challenges and capture the long-term growth opportunities in the Indian consumption story.

Let me begin by giving a quick snapshot of our financial performance. During the course of this
call, we will be referring to standalone financials.
During Q3 of FY26, the company delivered the highest ever revenue from operations of Rs.
10,483.71 crores, registering year-on-year growth of 16.53%. The total EBITDA, excluding the
exceptional items for the quarter, stood at Rs. 492.06 crores with a margin of 4.69%, while profit
before tax was Rs. 364.54 crores, translating into a PBT margin of 3.46%. Please note, the impact
of labour code during Q3 stood at Rs. 30.19 crores. This has been classified under the exceptional
items.
The company also delivered the highest ever revenue from operations for the 9 months of FY26,
with reported revenue from operations amounting to Rs. 29,013.98 crores. The total EBITDA,
excluding exceptional items for the period, was Rs. 1,429.56 crores, with a margin of 4.93%.
Profit before tax stood at Rs. 1,118.24 crores, translating into a PBT margin of approximately
3.84%.
Let me now give an overview of the operating environment of Q3 FY26:
Q3 FY26 was a period of transition and execution, largely influenced by the rollout of GST 2.0

Q3 FY26 was a period of transition and execution, largely influenced by the rollout of GST 2.0
reforms. The months of September and October experienced temporary trade disruptions due to
repricing actions, packaging updates, and operational adjustments. By November, inventory
levels began to stabilize. During the quarter, we introduced higher grammage packs, revised

pricing to pass on the GST-related benefits to consumers. We anticipate a stronger volume
recovery ahead, with the positive effects of GST rate reductions expected to become more
evident in the upcoming quarters.
The rural consumption continues to outperform urban demand for the seventh straight quarter.
However, we are now seeing a robust rebound in the urban consumption as well, supported by
rising disposable incomes, particularly benefiting the key food categories and the positive
impacts from revised direct and indirect taxation measures. This quarter was also benefited from
the festive season, with Diwali acting as a key demand catalyst across categories. Festive lead
purchases were supported by positive consumer sentiment, while the GST-led price corrections
improved affordability and further supported.
On the cost front, the palm oil prices declined materially by 12.6% on a year-on-year basis, with
a sequential moderation of 3.7% during the quarter. In December ‘25, the palm oil imports were
down 20%, while soybean oil imports increased by 20.2%, reflecting a shift in the edible oil
basket. Looking ahead, the pricing pressures are expected to persist amid tightening global
vegetable oil supplies. Wheat prices remained range-bound, with no significant movement

supported by comfortable supply levels in the physical markets. The government's intervention
schemes continued to effectively cap price increases. During Q3, sugar prices stayed firm, while
supply conditions remained comfortable, festive demand provided the price support.
Let me now walk you through the segment-wise performance during Q3 of FY26:
For the edible oil segment, the quarterly revenue stood at Rs. 7,335.71 crores, registering 8.98%
year-on-year growth with EBITDA margin for the segment was 2.39%. The primary growth
drivers in edible oil are branded oils such as Ruchi Gold, Mahakosh, and Sunrich. In the 9 months

nearly 85% of total edible oil sales now come from branded edible oils, driven by strong
marketing initiatives and impactful brand endorsements.
In Q3 FY26, the palm oil prices decreased considerably. India's palm oil imports fell to an 8-
month low in December, mainly due to seasonal demand and increased purchases of rival oils
such as soya oil and sunflower oil. India's palm oil imports typically moderated during the winter
months, as the tropical oil solidifies at lower temperatures, limiting its use in the northern parts

months, as the tropical oil solidifies at lower temperatures, limiting its use in the northern parts

Distribution remains the core strength of our business, and we continue to focus on expanding

Now commenting on the outlook:
From a demand perspective, we are hopeful that at the end of FY26 could be strong, primarily
supported by favorable macro tailwinds. The demand benefits are likely to accrue progressively
over the coming months, supported by improved affordability, wider distribution, and a
continued shift from unbranded to branded consumption. Together, these factors position the
company well to capture the incremental demand and deliver a stronger performance in the

demand is expected to strengthen in the coming quarters, aided by easing inflationary pressure

leading channels.
Now commenting on the outlook:
From a demand perspective, we are hopeful that at the end of FY26 could be strong, primarily
supported by favorable macro tailwinds. The demand benefits are likely to accrue progressively
over the coming months, supported by improved affordability, wider distribution, and a
continued shift from unbranded to branded consumption. Together, these factors position the
company well to capture the incremental demand and deliver a stronger performance in the
coming quarters. Further, GST 2.0 reforms are likely to stimulate consumption over time. Urban
demand is expected to strengthen in the coming quarters, aided by easing inflationary pressure
